column11: Nedarim 31a: ‘GEMARA: Concerning the mishna’s ruling that the one who takes such a vow is permitted to derive benefit from the nations of the world, the Gemara asks: But isn’t there Ishmael and his descendants, who are also Abraham’s offspring? column13: See Nachmanides on the verse: "a root bearing gall and wormwood" (Deuteronomy 29:17); therefore the Sages taught in Nedarim (31a): "'For in Isaac shall seed be called to you'—and not Esau or Ishmael," for they are not designated the seed of Abraham, since although he sired them biologically, his spiritual potency is not manifest in them following their birth, unless one converts, whereupon he is called "the son of Abraham," our Sages teaching (Berakhot 13a) that ultimately he became "a father to the entire world," the father of converts (Chagigah 3a).

column15: “And Isaac sowed in that land, and found in that same year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him” (Genesis 26:12). My grandfather (the Beit Yaakov) taught that the attribute of Isaac is sowing (zeri’ah): when a seed is planted in the ground, to the outward eye it appears to rot and dissolve completely, yet precisely from that dissolution springs forth a hundredfold harvest. So too, every contraction and humbling that a person undergoes in divine service is a sowing that yields manifold spiritual growth.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 17:5: ‘“The Lord God cast a deep slumber upon the man, and he slept. He took one of his sides, and He closed it with flesh in its place [taḥtena]” (Genesis 2:21). “The Lord God cast [hipil] a deep slumber” – Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin said in the name of Rabbi Levi: The beginning of downfall [mapala] is sleep. When a person sleeps, he does not toil in Torah and does not do any work. literally means, “He caused to fall down.” Rav said: There are three slumbers: the slumber of sleep, the slumber of prophecy, and the slumber of a trance. column11: Bava Batra 12a: ‘Rabba bar bar Ḥana says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: With regard to alleyways that are open to another city, and through which one would ordinarily travel to reach that other city, if the residents of the city in which the alleyways are located wished to block them off, the residents of the city into which the alleyways open can prevent them from doing so, because they have a right to reach their city via those routes. column15: “And they journeyed from Rephidim, and came to the wilderness of Sinai” (Exodus 19:2)—on which the Gemara (Bekhorot 5b) expounds that at Rephidim they slackened their hands from the words of Torah. Why did this stumbling occur immediately prior to the Giving of the Torah, just as “a person does not fully grasp words of Torah unless he has first stumbled in them” (Gittin 43a)? To show Israel that through the light of the Torah given at Sinai, every prior stumbling is repaired and transformed into deeper comprehension.

column15: “Return, O Israel, unto the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity” (Hosea 14:2; Yoma 86b). Thus even a willful transgression is called a ‘stumbling’ once the light of return shines.

column11: Berakhot 5b: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan said to him: What is your source for this? column11: Chullin 89a: ‘The Gemara relates: Rava says, and some say Rabbi Yoḥanan says: Greater is that which is stated with regard to Moses and Aaron than that which is stated with regard to Abraham. And Rava says, and some say Rabbi Yoḥanan says: The world endures only in the merit of Moses and Aaron. It is written here: “And what are we,” and it written elsewhere: “He hangs the earth upon nothing” (Job 26:7). That is, the earth endures in the merit of those who said of themselves that they are nothing, i.e., Moses and Aaron.’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chullin 89a) to illuminate his exposition here (“regarding which he said: "and I am but dust and ashes" [Genesis 18:27], as the Sages explained [Chullin 89a], matching Jacob's "I am unworthy of all the mercies" [Genesis 32:11], recognizing his utter lowliness...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the themes of prayer, barrenness and spiritual fruitfulness, and the Oral Torah developed in Poked Akarim.

column11: Sanhedrin 109a: ‘It was taught in a baraita: “Wicked” is referring to sins they committed with their money; “and sinners” is referring to sins they committed with their bodies. “Wicked” is referring to sins they committed with their money, as it is written: “And your eye is wicked against your poor brother and you give him nothing” (Deuteronomy 15:9). “And sinners” is referring to sins they committed with their bodies, as it is written with regard to Joseph and the wife of Potiphar: “And sin against God” (Genesis 39:9). “Before the Lord”; this is referring to blessing, a euphemism for cursing, God. “Exceedingly [meod ]” is referring to bloodshed, as it is stated: “Moreover Manasseh shed very [meod ] much…’ Context and connection to Poked Akarim: In Poked Akarim 4, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 109a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as the Sages stated: "You gave tranquility to the wicked..."
